concepts.description: Redis stores all data in memory for fast access

concepts.name: Key-Value Store
concepts.description: Data is stored using key-value pairs
characteristics: Values can be different data types

topics.title: Caching Patterns

patterns.name: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
patterns.description: Load data into cache only when necessary

advantages: Resilient to cache failures (cache down means slower, not broken)
Simple to implement; default choice for most systems
disadvantages: Data can become stale (bound staleness with TTL)
Susceptible to cache stampede on hot key expiry

patterns.name: Write-Through
patterns.description: Write to cache and DB simultaneously

patterns.name: Write-Behind
patterns.description: Write to cache and asynchronously update DB

patterns.name: Read-Through
patterns.description: The cache itself loads data from the database on a miss

disadvantages: Requires cache library/provider with loader support
notes: Spring @Cacheable provides read-through behavior at the method level

patterns.name: Refresh-Ahead
patterns.description: Re-load popular keys before TTL expiry

advantages: Hot keys never expire under load
disadvantages: Wasted refreshes for keys that stop being accessed
notes: Use for hot keys with predictable access patterns

topics.write_strategy_note: Update vs delete on write: prefer delete (invalidate) - recomputing on next read avoids the race where two writers store stale values in the wrong order. TTL remains as the safety net.

topics.title: Cache Failure Modes
topics.description: Classic caching failure modes interviewers expect you to name unprompted

concepts.name: Stampede / Thundering Herd
concepts.description: A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database simultaneously
solutions: Per-key lock (single flight - one loader, the rest wait)

concepts.name: Penetration
concepts.description: Requests for keys that never exist bypass the cache every time
solutions: Cache negative results with a short TTL
Bloom filter in front of the cache

concepts.name: Avalanche
concepts.description: Many keys expire at once, e.g. after a deploy warmed them together

concepts.name: Hot Key
concepts.description: One celebrity key overloads a single Redis node

concepts.name: Inconsistency Window
concepts.description: Between the DB write and the cache delete, a reader can cache stale data
solutions: Don't cache data where staleness costs money

strategies.name: Event-Driven Sync
strategies.description: Use database events to update cache

@Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id", sync = true)

examples.description: Update cache without skipping the method

considerations: Same-class self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so the cache annotation is ignored (same trap as @Transactional)

concepts.name: Single-Threaded Model
concepts.description: Redis runs a single-threaded event loop: commands are atomic, no lock contention, I/O multiplexing (epoll), efficient data structures. I/O threads since Redis 6 help with network handling, but command execution stays single-threaded.
characteristics: Every command is atomic for free

concepts.name: Eviction Policies (maxmemory-policy)
concepts.description: What Redis does when memory is full
policies: allkeys-lru: evict least-recently-used keys - best for pure caches
volatile-lru / volatile-ttl: only evict keys that have a TTL - use when Redis also stores non-evictable data
noeviction (default): writes fail when memory is full

concepts.name: Persistence
concepts.description: Optional durability mechanisms
options: RDB snapshots: fast restart, may lose the last minutes of writes
AOF (append-only file): logs every write, configurable fsync
Pure cache: turning persistence off entirely is legitimate

concepts.name: High Availability & Scaling
concepts.description: Replication and sharding options
options: Replication: primary to replicas, plus Sentinel for automatic failover
Redis Cluster: shards data by hash slots (16384 slots)
Multi-key operations in Cluster must share a slot - use hash tags like {user:42}

concepts.name: Distributed Lock
concepts.description: SET lock:order:42 token NX PX 30000, released via a Lua compare-and-delete script
notes: The Redlock algorithm across multiple nodes is debated - mention this in interviews

concepts.name: Rate Limiting
concepts.description: INCR + EXPIRE for a fixed window, or a sorted-set sliding window for accuracy

concepts.name: Session Store
concepts.description: Spring Session Redis lets application instances stay stateless

concepts.name: Pub/Sub and Streams
concepts.description: PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE for fire-and-forget notifications; Streams (XADD) provide a lightweight Kafka-like persistent log

concepts.name: Two-Level Caching
concepts.description: Caffeine (in-JVM L1, microsecond access) in front of Redis (shared L2). Keep the levels coherent with pub/sub invalidation events.

concepts.name: Walk me through cache-aside and its consistency guarantees.
concepts.description: Read: cache, then on miss read the DB and populate the cache with a TTL. Write: DB first, then delete the key. Guarantees: eventual consistency bounded by TTL; a small race window exists - acceptable for most reads, not for balances.

concepts.name: How do you prevent a cache stampede?
concepts.description: Per-key mutex/single-flight (@Cacheable(sync=true) or Redis SETNX), serve stale content while one thread refreshes, jittered TTLs so keys do not expire together.

concepts.name: Why is Redis fast despite being single-threaded?
concepts.description: Everything is in memory, there is no lock contention (one command at a time gives atomicity for free), I/O multiplexing (epoll), and efficient data structures. I/O threads since Redis 6 help with network handling; command execution stays single-threaded.

concepts.name: What would you cache in a typical e-commerce backend - and what not?
concepts.description: Cache: product catalog, categories, rendered fragments, sessions, config and feature flags. Do not cache: stock levels at checkout, payment state, anything where staleness costs money - or cache with explicit invalidation and a very short TTL.

concepts.name: Local (Caffeine) vs distributed (Redis) cache?
concepts.description: Local: nanosecond access, no network hop, but per-instance duplication and incoherence across instances. Distributed: shared, consistent view that survives deploys, at the cost of a network hop. Standard answer: use both, layered.
